precepts.text: When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it, for he hath no pleasure in fools; better it is that thou shouldest not vow than that thou shouldest vow and not pay, and say not before the angel that it was an error.
precepts.point: The lesson the Most High is teaching Israel here is to pay what you vow. Let your yea be yea and your nay be nay; Saul went back on his word after he had given his yea to the Amorites, and the whole house paid for it.

note.label: 2 Samuel 21: The Famine, the Gibeonites, and the Sons of the Giant

precepts.why:
“When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.” And “neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error”.

That is the lesson of the famine. It lasted “three years, year after year”, and when David enquired, “the Lord answered, It is for Saul, and for his bloody house, because he slew the Gibeonites.” The Gibeonites “were not of the children of Israel, but of the remnant of the Amorites; and the children of Israel had sworn unto them”, yet Saul sought to slay them in his zeal. Saul broke his word.

David asked, “wherewith shall I make the atonement, that ye may bless the inheritance of the Lord?” The blessing was not truly coming from the Gibeonites; it was coming from the Most High, who was teaching Israel a lesson through this famine. They would have “no silver nor gold of Saul, nor of his house”, but asked for seven of his sons to hang up unto the Lord in Gibeah of Saul. Saul did not pay what was vowed, and the whole house paid for it.

precepts.text: Christ simplified it: let your communication be yea, yea, nay, nay, for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.
precepts.point: The lesson the Most High is teaching Israel here is to pay what you vow. Let your yea be yea and your nay be nay; Saul went back on his word after he had given his yea to the Amorites, and the whole house paid for it.

note.label: 2 Samuel 21: The Famine, the Gibeonites, and the Sons of the Giant

precepts.why:
“But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.” Christ simplified it.

Let your yea be yea and your nay be nay. Saul went back on his word after he had given his yea to the Amorites, and the Lord sent three years of famine for it, until seven of Saul’s sons were given up to be hanged unto the Lord. The lesson the Most High is teaching Israel here is to pay what you vow.

note.label: 2 Samuel 21: The Famine, the Gibeonites, and the Sons of the Giant

precepts.why:
“It is God that girdeth me with strength, and maketh my way perfect. He maketh my feet like hinds’ feet, and setteth me upon my high places. He teacheth my hands to war, so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms.” That is the strength the Most High gave David in his youth.

Now David was getting up in age. The Philistines had war again with Israel, “and David waxed faint.” Ishbi-benob, of the sons of the giant, “thought to have slain David. But Abishai the son of Zeruiah succoured him, and smote the Philistine, and killed him.” Then David’s men swore, “Thou shalt go no more out with us to battle, that thou quench not the light of Israel.” It was time for him to sit on the throne.

His servants finished the work. At Gob and at Gath the sons of the giant fell: Sibbechai the Hushathite slew one, Elhanan slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite, “the staff of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam”, and Jonathan the son of Shimea, David’s brother, slew a man of great stature “that had on every hand six fingers, and on every foot six toes”. These were tall men, one about eight or nine feet, not the twenty foot giants of fairy tales. Goliath had kin, and “These four were born to the giant in Gath, and fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants.”

points: The king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, because of the Lord's oath that was between David and Jonathan. David did not go back on his oath; earlier he had promised Jonathan that his seed would always eat at David's table as long as there was family of the lineage of Jonathan.

note.label: 2 Samuel 21: The Famine, the Gibeonites, and the Sons of the Giant

points: But the king took the two sons of Rizpah and the five sons of Michal and delivered them into the hands of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them in the hill before the Lord. They fell all seven together and were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, in the beginning of barley harvest.

note.label: 2 Samuel 21: The Famine, the Gibeonites, and the Sons of the Giant

points: Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, took sackcloth and spread it upon the rock from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and she suffered neither the birds of the air by day nor the beasts of the field by night to touch them. When David was told, he went and took the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, which had stolen them from the street of Beth-shan where the Philistines had hanged them when Saul was slain in Gilboa.

note.label: 2 Samuel 21: The Famine, the Gibeonites, and the Sons of the Giant

points: Jonathan's body had been hanged in the temple of Dagon, the fish god of the Hamites. David buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan in the country of Benjamin in Zelah, in the sepulchre of Kish his father, and performed all that the king commanded. After that the Most High was entreated for the land.
